The house resumed from Wednesday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacNeil:
That the agreement between the government and the John Inglis Company, of Toronto, for the manufacture of Bren machine guns, the report of the royal commission dealing with said agreement, and all related documents, evidence, vouchers and exhibits, be referred to the standing committee on public accounts; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stevens.
Mr. A. MacG. YOUNG (Saskatoon): Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock last evening I was discussing the Bren gun contract and pointing out the very strange tactics of the opposition. I should like in the few minutes I have left to sum up the argument I was making.
The motion before the house is to refer to the public accounts committee the Bren gun ;ontract and the report of the royal commission in regard thereto, so that it may be fully investigated, if further investigation be necessary. The Conservative party has very strenuously opposed the motion. Why, then, do they not accept the verdict of Mr. Justice Davis, the commissioner, who said that he could not find any evidence of wrongdoing on the part of the minister, his deputy, or any other official, or any member of the House of Commons or of the Senate? The commissioner went further and said-this is the limit to which any man could go-that there was not even a suspicion of any wrongdoing. This is the finest testimonial of character and high purpose which any man could receive.
As to form and substance of the contract the commissioner did say, "upon the whole

evidence, that is a question for the government and parliament to pass upon." Let us accept that view. Then what should we do? What has always been the practice in this house when a particular matter had to be investigated? Send it to a committee, of course, where all the evidence given before the commission could be studied and, in this case, in addition the further evidence which is now available. From press reports which I read carefully I noted that the commissioner did not think it necessary to admit evidence to say how good the contract was. I most certainly have no criticism to offer on that account. His conception of his duty was to find out if there was any wrongdoing on the part of anyone, not to find out how good the contract was. He found there was no wrongdoing or suspicion of wrongdoing on the part of the minister, his officials or any member of the House of Commons or of the Senate.
There is much evidence to be submitted to show this contract to be an excellent contract, and this is the reason why the leader of the opposition and his party do not wish this whole matter to go before the committee. They know that after all the evidence is heard the public will brand their speeches in this house this week, filled as they were with insinuations and veiled accusations, as being of a type used by cheap Tammany ward politicians. If there is honesty of purpose in their actions they should all vote to send this to the committee where the whole facts can be reviewed and where witnesses will have the right and the opportunity to be heard. Their tactics will be condemned not only by this house but by the people of this country.
Many references have been made to the fact that there was no competitive bidding on the contract. What did government counsel propose doing before the commission about this? They wished to bring contractors from this country and the United States to prove that in a contract such as the Bren gun contract competitive bidding would be impossible of accomplishment. The witnesses were all present and ready to give evidence. After considering this proposal the commissioner decided against calling such witnesses, and so did Colonel Drew. The experience of Great Britain for over a hundred years demonstrates clearly that in such cases competitive bids are impossible.
In conclusion let me say to the leader of the opposition and to his party:	In the interests of this country, stop this petty quibbling, these unwarranted insinuations. After all, the Conservative party in the past has had a noble tradition. The hon.

Bren Gun-Mr. Howe
gentleman is a new leader; let me suggest to him that he start on a high plane, and not in cheap ward politics. His party is really worthy of a better effort than is now being displayed.

the strangest that has taken place since I came into this house, and I believe it is one of the strangest on record. A magazine article appeared which caused a good deal of comment. The article confined itself to vague insinuations; it made no charge of wrongdoing.	However, the government felt that

we have had hon. gentlemen opposite discussing this matter for several days. Here again each member who gets up is careful to say that he makes no charge of wrongdoing. We have heard from the opposition only vague charges of inefficiency in dealing with this contract, and a blackguarding of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). It is with the charge of inefficiency in connection with this contract that I wish to deal.
I may sav. and I think all hon. gentlemen will agree with me, that the purchase of arms and munitions has always been a difficult matter for a government to deal with, and the situation is far more difficult in peace time than it is in war time. In time of war, a volume of munitions can be contracted for which will warrant the setting up of the particular equipment and organization required for the production. Most of the buying for my own department, and I imagine the same thing applies to other departments of government, is a comparatively simple matter because generally the articles being purchased are in ordinary commercial use and are such as can be secured from the general stock of the manufacturer. But no one stocks arms and munitions of warfare of the type useful in the situation that confronts us at present. The result is that it is necessary to make special arrangements for the manufacture of these articles.
I have had some experience with this type of purchasing. Like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) I received a training as an engineer, but unlike the hon. member for Greenwood I practised my profession for many years. I practised it in a highly specialized field and in that practice I had to purchase equipment which was not of standard manufacture, but which had to be designed in my own draughting room and constructed in the factories of Canada. It so happens that a large portion of that equipment was manufactured in the particular plant under discussion, the plant of the John Inglis Company of Toronto. We have heard it referred to as a broken down plant, but I know it as one of the best equipped of the boiler plants and machine shops in the Dominion of Canada. In my practice it was one of three plants in Canada which was capable of turning out a large order of mechanical equipment for a grain elevator. In my practice it has supplied equipment of that type worth several hundreds of thousands of dollars. I took enough interest in the matter a short time ago to visit this so-called decrepit and broken-down plant, because I wished to confirm my opinion that it was still capable of efficient production. To my surprise I found
Bren Gun-Mr. Howe

that the Bren gun was not being made in the Inglis plant as I knew it. That plant was being used for the purposes for which it had always been used, the normal production of boilers and special types of mechanical equipment. But I found that a new plant had been built as an addition to the Inglis plant, and that this addition was of most modern factory construction, of concrete, and with the best of ventilating and lighting systems, and I learned that the Bren machine gun was to be manufactured in that new portion of the plant. I found that that plant was being filled with the special machinery required to carry out the Bren gun contract, with the most modem lay-out that could be used for that type of production. This, then, was the broken-down plant that has been referred to so frequently by hon. gentlemen opposite in this debate.

There is one thing that I wish to call to the attention of the house, and that is that at this moment all of us are defence-minded. We have all seen the threat of war come almost to the boiling point and then cool down, and we have all felt very thankful that something was being done to provide an adequate defence for this country. I just wish to remind hon. members that it was the present Minister of National Defence who started the machinery which is bringing Canada into a position in which she can defend herself against attack.
Now let us examine the particular transaction under consideration from the point of view of lack of efficiency. In 1933 Lieutenant Jolley was sent to England to investigate the small arms situation. In August, 1935, he visited the Enfield plant in England, which was just then beginning to set up for the manufacture of the Bren gun. In July, 1936, Lieutenant Jolley returned to Canada and reported to his department that the Bren gun was a distinct advance on other types of machine guns and would be the type required in Canada for defence purposes.
Some two months later, two machine guns were received in Canada from Czechoslovakia,

I should be interested if someone would pick out the substance and separate it from the form.
It has been taken for granted in this house that the contractor will receive as a result of his work a profit of about 7-6 per cent on his cost. I am not prepared to admit even that, because I notice a clause in the contract having to do with rejects. The contract provides that unless the number of rejects can be kept down to that of other plants in efficient operation, the cost of those rejects can be charged up to the contractor, and, in fact, his whole plant taken over and the contract completed by others. It seems to me that is a hazard, and a very serious hazard, to those who hold this contract, and one that might very easily call for insurance in the margin of profit allowed.
Having had some experience in placing these contracts, I venture to say that no manufacturer in Canada, who has a plant in actual production, would want that kind of contract. I have put it to a number of my friends in the manufacturing business, and I have never found one who, when he was pinned down to it, would admit that he would take this contract into his plant. I met in Ottawa one or two contractors who came here prepared to give their evidence before the inquiry that they would not want that type of contract in their plant, and that it was not a favourable contract as far as the contractor is concerned.
So much for the charge of inefficiency against the minister. We all know that when

a department is stepped up, from the level at which this department was operating in 1933 and 1934, to two and a half times the former expenditure, all details in that department may not be handled efficiently. When a departmental budget is enlarged to four or five times the size it was a few years ago, some additions of course are necessary. The Minister of National Defence had called the attention of the government to the fact that his purchasing staff was inadequate to handle the volume of work thrown upon it, and himself had suggested such a purchasing board as was in vogue in 1917. Mr. Justice Davis recommended in his report that type of board. I am sure that no hon. member on this side of the house, and least of all the Minister of National Defence, would quarrel with that finding of Commissioner Davis. Just how that can be twisted into a charge of inefficiency against the minister I am at a loss to understand.

My hon. friend says that it has made one man the leader of the Tory party in Ontario; and I think that that fact has so strongly impressed itself upon others in tuis house that it has had a good deal to do with the length of this debate. One thing it certainly has done: it has tended to prevent the government from arriving at its goal of obtaining 7,000 Bren machine guns. The hon. member for Kootenay East said that if it had not been for hon. gentlemen opposite, this contract would now have been working smoothly. I am glad to be able to tell him, in consequence of my call at the plant, that the contract is working smoothly. I was told there that it was expected that parts for the Bren machine gun would be produced next June, fifteen months after the signing of the contract. So it has not had the effect it reasonably could have had in slowing down production on this particular contract; rather, it has had the effect of stopping the flow of orders from Great Britain for munitions manufactured in this country. Before this inquiry started munition orders were flowing here, small orders, it is true, because the buying of munitions in peace time must necessarily be made through small orders. If Canada should not be called upon to go to war, the present purchase of 7,000 Bren machine guns may last for a decade or two. If war comes, an immediate production of many times 7,000 will be required. No small part of the defence

Bren Gun-Mr. Stewart
of Canada is in building up the productive capacity of manufacturing plants to be available in time of war.
At the completion of this contract we shall have a plant built specially for the manufacture of Bren machine guns. When this contract is finished the plant will be turned to other uses, tout if at any time in the future more Bren machine guns are required, we shall have the plant that built them, the machinery that was used in their manufacture, and we will place that plant in production in short order. That is an important part of Canadian defence.
When Britain places an order for munitions or for aeroplanes to be manufactured in Canada the output is for Great Britain, but it does this for Canada: it establishes plants in Canada with productive capacity available to Canada in time of need; and whatever may be said about British orders in this country as a contribution towards relieving unemployment, they have a real use to Canada as a defensive weapon. It is a calamity to this country that this flow of orders from Great Britain should be stopped. If for no other reason, this matter of the Bren gun should be allowed to drop, and the defence department permitted to get on with its business, which is so important to the safety of the country at this time.
I could perhaps discuss some of the side issues-how much stock was sold and at what price; but what has that to do with the production of Bren machine guns? Does the buyer examine the financing of a company before placing an order with it? What a buyer is interested in is the productive capacity of a plant and the ability of the management to fill his order. If stock was sold, the sale of that stock was regulated not by this government but rather by the provincial government. A statement was made that there were street rumours in Montreal that the stock would sell at $20 a share. Those rumours could have been dispelled quickly if people had looked up the ruling of the Ontario securities commission limiting the sale price to $7.50 a share. I should be glad-but, no; I will not say anything more about rumours. I might have to retract.
I do not wish to pursue the matter further, but I do submit that the Minister of National Defence has been unfairly attacked from the point of view of efficiency in connection with this Bren machine gun order. I suggest that the requests for his resignation are an attack upon him personally which is not justified by anything that has happened in respect to this order. I sincerely hope that hon. gentlemen opposite will examine their position and ask
themselves whether they are doing something worth while for Canada in keeping up this propaganda. I trust that the defence plans of the country will be no longer held back because of this discussion.

I hope
to be able to address the house briefly upon this important subject without calling names, without questioning motives, and dealing only with facts. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) has taken another course; I do not propose to follow his example. He spoke about the appropriations in years gone by for defence purposes and compared them with the appropriations that have been made dur< ing the past few years.
Let me point out to him and to this house that the conditions are altogether different. When the appropriations to which he refers were made, the program of the British empire and of the dominions was, as he knows perfectly well, in the direction of disarmament. That is the program that was supposed to be in effect throughout the world. be no more uncertainty and futility. Let us choose between futility and finality in connection with this issue. Let us get it over with.
I was surprised that when the Prime Minister read this report he did not at once take proceedings to have the contract cancelled. I cannot think of anything that would have done more to restore public confidence in his government and in the Department of National Defence. The contract contains certain provisions dealing with possible cancellation. They are vague and indefinite, but I have no doubt that cancellation could be made on terms that would be fair to the contractor. At the same time that the contract is cancelled, let the doors of the courts be opened to the contractor, and if his hands are clean he can obtain damages or compensation on the basis provided for in the contract.
One firm and one firm only had a chance to tender for this contract. Let me ask three or four questions. Why was the recommendation of the British government that these munitions be manufactured in a government arsenal disregarded? Why were tenders not invited? Why was Major Hahn introduced to the department as he was, and why was he introduced by the department and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the British government and given a preferred position over all others? There is only one answer that fits all these questions, and that answer is consistent with the action taken by this government. From the beginning it was the determination and intention to give this contract to Major Hahn and to no other person. That is the only answer that is consistent with the whole record and with the findings of the commissioner.
I contend that having regard to the present state of public opinion with respect to profits from war expenditures that is a very bad situation. The public desire competition in the letting of contracts, and they are particularly insistent on that in respect of contracts having to do with war expenditures. In my opinion the best way to restore the confidence of the public would be to wash the slate clean and start all over on a sound basis of public competition or competition by a selected number of firms capable of doing work of this kind. This contract was given to a firm which had no experience, no plant and no equipment. Everything points to a determination and intention on the part of the government to give the contract to one firm and one firm only.
What should be done under the circumstances? I submit that this is not a matter for further investigation by the public ac-

I have the utmost respect for the public accounts committee, but I repeat that a reference to that committee without instructions would be pure futility. It will get us nowhere. The report will come back to the house in the dying days of the session and we will be faced with the veiy situation that faces us to-day. Let us clean it up now. That is, that he could not make a report definitely implicating anybody or charging anybody with wrongdoing.
-as well as the weighty consideration brought to my attention by counsel that the rights of the individuals interested in the contract might become the subject of legal controversy elsewhere, I have come to the conclusion that it is inexpedient to comment upon the evidence in respect of its bearing on the conduct of the individuals concerned.
Not because there was nothing to comment on, but because, in his opinion, it was inexpedient so to comment. It seems abundantly clear to me that the reason the commissioner did not comment on the evidence was that to do so was not within the terms of the commission given him. However, in my opinion the commissioner did comment by inference, and commented so clearly that they who run may read and they who read may run. I read the report when it was first
tabled; I have, of course, referred again and again to certain parts of it since this debate began, and I am convinced that in his report, which, considering the length of the inquiry and the volume of the evidence, is a brief one, the commissioner dealt only with the pertinent issues in the investigation.
Naturally the steps leading to the signing of the contract are first touched on. The commissioner points out that the British government had acquired from the patentee the rights to manufacture the Bren gun, and that by the terms of the agreement the governments of the dominions had the right to manufacture the guns provided that they were manufactured in a factory or factories operated by the governments concerned. The report reads:
"The privilege of so doing-
That is, the privilege of producing the gun in Canada.
-was vouchsafed to the Canadian government by the war office w'hen it acquired the rights of manufacture from the patentee, the only stipulation being that such production must take place in a government-owned factory."
The commissioner then refers to the information which the Department of National Defence had or could have had with regard to the Bren gun. He refers at length to Lieutenant Jolley, of the Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps. This reference to Lieutenant Jolley is significant, because he gives to this one phase two pages of the fifty pages which constitute the report. He sets forth this officer's qualifications and experience, and states, on page 6:
During his study at Enfield, the Bren gun was not actually in the process of production, but plants were being made for its production at that time. "They were working crut the design of tools, fixtures, gauges, etc., and were planning the actual system or series of operations on each component which was to be used when the factory went into production on the Bren gun." They had not progressed sufficiently far to give him any indication as to the quantities of machines which they would require or to give him any details of the processes of production. However, he did get the range and types of machines which they were planning to use in the production of Bren guns. He saw the gun complete and studied it in detail "from the point of view of the design characteristics of the gun and the tolerances of the components and the general requirements of the finished gun." He put the date of his study of the Bren gun as June, 1936. He said he was particularly interested in the Bren gun because it was a new weapon that had just been adopted something like a year before (speaking of June, 1936) and everyone was very keen about it in Enfield as well as in other parts of England. He said he wanted to get as much information as he could, not only of the gun itself, but also of the production methods in case it might be required at some future date. Lieutenant Jolley, assumed
Bren Gun-Mr. Maclnnis

that it 'was quite likely that the .Bren gun would become standard equipment in Canada at some future time. He returned to Canada in August, 1936, with a general working knowledge of what might be expected if the Bren gun were to be produced in Canada. With the possible exception of other officers who had attended courses in England, he was the only Canadian officer who had seen the Bren gun at that time, as far as he knew.. Lieutenant Jolley has been employed since his return in the office of the Master-General of Ordnance.
Then the commissioner points out:
The Department of National Defence therefore had, on the return of Lieutenant Jolley from England in August, 1936, very considerable knowledge and information available to it for the consideration of the problem of the production in Canada of its actual requirements of Bren guns.
Despite that fact-I am quoting again from the report:
No contract for the purchase or production of the Canadian defence requirements of the Bren machine gun was made however until March 31st, 1938, when a contract was made between the Canadian government and John Inglis Company Limited of Toronto, a company incorporated and organized by Major J. E. Hahn and associates.
Why all this delay? From what later transpired and what has now been brought out, obviously the cause of the delay was that the Department of National Defence was so busy from August, 1936, to November, 1937, putting pressure on the British war office to allow the manufacture of Bren guns in a private factory, so that a special, selected contractor could get his feet in into the patronage trough, that they had no time to get on with the business of organizing, with the knowledge and information available, for production in a government-owned plant.
Hon. members opposite accuse us of delaying or hampering the production of munitions. We are not responsible for the delay; it took place long before we had any knowledge of what was going on.
The commissioner then comments on the fact that although the contract involved several millions of dollars, competitive tenders were not called. His own words, appearing on page 8 of the report, are these:
Notwithstanding that the contract involves the expenditure of several millions of dollars by the Canadian government, no industrial producer (other than Major Hahn) was consulted by the Department of National Defence as to the proposed manufacture of Bren guns for the Canadian government or invited to give competitive bids or terms of manufacture. Nor did anyone, so far as the evidence shows, ever visit any industrial plant (except Inglis) to consider the possibility of production of Bren guns in Canada.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is an amazing situation. For notwithstanding the factors

concerned, not the slightest attempt was made to get competitive bids, although several million dollars were involved. The commissioner did not comment on the conduct of persons, but in my opinion this paragraph in the report speaks volumes and it is one of the reasons why the report should be referred to the public accounts committee, to see whether we cannot find out the causes underlying this strange way of carrying on public business. The reason given by the Minister of National Defence in his evidence for this remarkable state of affairs passes all understanding and knowledge. The commissioner must have thought the reason strange. He emphasized it in the report. He calls attention to the question asked by Mr. Hell-muth:
You did not give anybody else a chance?
And the minister's reply was: "Nobody asked for it." I have not the pleasure of Mr. Justice Davis's acquaintance and I do not know how he would react when faced with an answer such as this, but I am almost sure that he must have made some inaudible, but emphatic comment. Could hon. members before this report appeared imagine a responsible minister giving such a childish naive answer to the question why government business totalling several million dollars was given to a favoured company without an attempt being made even to inquire whether other firms could do the work? Are we to understand that is to be the future policy of the government with reference to government contracts and business? If it is not to be the future policy of the government, why was it followed on this occasion? Are we to understand that before anyone can get business from this government he must be introduced by a Liberal member of parliament and have friends inside the service to push his case? That way of doing business is bad at any time and under any circumstances, but it is most heinous in a matter such as this.
The minister said that he favoured public ownership in connection with the manufacture of armaments, and he says that he still maintains that position. But his activities do not square with his assertions. He favours public ownership; that is what he says; and failing that he favours competition. But he ends up by adopting a policy which is neither public ownership nor competition but unadulterated patronage. He then tries to hide behind a smoke screen which he has laid himself-that he could not get the money. The commissioner however does not let him get out of sight. Of course, he does not comment; he

Bren Gun-Mr. Maclnnis
merely states the facts. I will read from the report. The commissioner's remarks will be found at pages 10 and 11:
The minister said that there were two very definite schools of thought in the department and that he assumed all responsibility. One school, he said, was headed by the then chief of general staff and the other by the deputy minister, for both of whom he said he had equally great admiration.
Evidently the chief of general staff did not have as much influence as the deputy minister of the department
The minister said that General Ashton (the then chief of the general staff) was very insistent upon the development of government arsenals and that the former chief of general staff, General McNaughton, evolved a very comprehensive scheme for Valcartier which would include practically all the requirements of the Canadian forces.
What he said was:
That was considered after I went into the department and I found that the cost of it would be something between $30,000,000 and $35,000,000. With my meagre $25,000,000 or $30,000,000, what could I do with a scheme like that?
The commissioner does not let him get away with that, although he does not make any comment on personal conduct. The commissioner says:
But the testimony given before the commission established that only 60,000 square feet of space was necessary for the purpose of production of the 7,000 Bren guns for Canada, as well as 5,000 guns for the war office, and that an entirely new building (apart from land) would cost approximately $120,000. In proposal \B" of Major Hahn (exhibit 11) of December 29, 1936, the building was shown at an estimated cost of $104,196.40.

That is the smoke screen. The minister is speaking of a complete plant, but this is not necessarily a complete plant. It is only a small part, and instead of requiring thirty or thirty-five millions, or two hundred or three hundred millions, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said the other evening, it would take very much less. Possibly a million and a half or two millions would have started the thing going and we would be very much further ahead than we are now. It is pointed out to me that the commissioner said $104,000, but that is for the building. And in any event the Canadian government and the British government are paying for the machinery, and we do not know what it will cost.
This brings me to the queer case of Major Hahn. The appointment of Major Hahn as the government's representative at the war office in Great Britain is to me one of the most amazing things in the political history of Canada. First we hear of the major when he is introduced to the deputy minister, General LaFleche, by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton). According to the evidence General LaFleche had not previously met or had any communication with Major Hahn. This introduction of Major Hahn to the deputy minister took place on October 9, 1936. A few days afterwards we find that the Minister of National Defence had his first meeting with Major Hahn. He was introduced by the member for Trinity on October 19, 1936. On this occasion, according to Major Hahn's own evidence at page 18 of the report, he met the minister and said he was going to England and that he wanted a letter, and he got the letter. The minister had never seen the man before and when questioned some time later he did not remember having met him or having given him the letter. Consequently Major Hahn did not make much of an impression on the minister, which seems very strange.
Now we come to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister had never met Major Hahn at all-I do not know whether he has met him yet. He did not even have the opportunity or pleasure of an introduction by the hon. member for Trinity yet we find the Prime Minister in his capacity as Secretary of State for External Affairs, on November 6, 1936, sending the following cablegram to the Canadian high commissioner in London:
Secret. Your cablegram 9th November 396. Have discussed matter with Minister of National Defence. You might request war office to give Major Hahn, as representing Canadian government in this particular, any information which they consider desirable and necessary to enable national defence to reach conclusion on possibility produce Bren gun in Canada. It is not desired to request furnishing of information on any article other than this gun.
It will be noted that the cablegram is marked " secret I do not know why. It was sent in code by the Prime Minister, and made Major Hahn a representative of the Canadian government at London, where he would have access to secrets of the war office.

speechtext:
But in view of the fact that no one knew who Major Hahn was I do not see the reason for the secrecy. That is the peculiar part about the whole thing. It is like the babes in the wood.
Now these are facts which cannot be contradicted: that the Prime Minister had never met Major Hahn and did not know anything about him except what he may have ascertained from the Minister of National Defence; that the Minister of National Defence did not know anything about Major Hahn except what he had heard from his deputy minister; that the deputy minister did not know anything about him except what he had heard from the hon. member for Trinity or was told by Major Hahn himself, as he said on the witness stand. Yet the proceedings were characterized by the utmost formality and secrecy. I have on occasions taken part in mock parliaments, but it seems to me this sort of thing reduces ordered government to a mockery and the administration of public business to a farce.
I mentioned earlier in my remarks that pressure was brought to bear on the British war office by the Department of National Defence, first, to allow the Bren gun to be produced by a private company, and, second, to have the war office place an order for 5,000 guns with a private company. That assertion is borne out by the commissioner's report at page 48, where he said:
It clearly results from the evidence that the department having introduced and" sponsored Hahn to the war office and the war office having in November 1937 (after a full year of pressure by the department upon it) expressed its readiness to negotiate with the Inglis company for the production of 5,000 guns, and the negotiations having proceeded to the point where on February 9, 1938 (exhibit 218) a draft contract with the John Inglis Company had been agreed in detail by the war office, the matter had been brought into such a posture that the department felt it was really not in a position to propose to the war office the consideration of another contractor.

That is why the interdepartmental committee fell down. And the year lost in putting pressure upon the war office is also the reason we are so far behind as we are at the present time.
In conclusion I wish to read the recommendation made by the commissioner, found on page 51 of the report. The minister and the government and the Liberal party claim that this recommendation exonerates the minister and the department from any and all blame in connection with this contract. In my opinion this, taken with the other points which I have dealt with, constitutes the most emphatic condemnation of the minister and the department. The commissioner states:
What is plain to me at the end of this long inquiry is this: that if the policy of private manufacture of war munitions and armaments is to be continued in this country (a question of administrative policy for the government and parliament to determine), once the requirements are determined by the Department of National Defence the negotiations leading up to and the making of contracts between the government and private manufacturers either for the purchase or production of such munitions or armaments should be put into the hands of an expert advisory group of competent business men

He goes on to state the kind of business men he has in mind, and continues:
These persons should constitute a board (which might be known as the "defence purchasing board") and be made directly accountable to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Finance.
We must bear in mind that the commissioner was inquiring into a contract which came under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence. After careful and prolonged inquiry he recommends in effect that, if there are to be any more contracts, the negotiating of them should be transferred to the Department of Finance, or to a department directly under the Prime Minister himself. In my opinion this clearly indicates that the commissioner was not satisfied with the contract or the way in which it was negotiated by the Department of National Defence, of which the minister is the political head. That is the inference I draw from it. The report gives a very clear indication of what the commissioner would say, had he not thought, as he said, that it would be inexpedient to comment on the evidence in respect of its bearing on the conduct of the individuals concerned.
It is for these reasons that we of this group maintain that it is in the public interest that this contract and all related material should be referred to the standing committee on public accounts for further investigation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to declare my position before

the house in this matter. The motion which has been made for further investigation is thought by many to be unnecessary. However, a further investigation is to be held. I shall welcome it as I welcomed the previous investigation. I shall be available before the public accounts committee at all times when I may be required. I shall be glad to testify either under o-ath or under my responsibility as a member of the House of Commons.
It has been indicated by the Prime Minister (MV Mackenzie Ring) that the proposed motion to refer the matter to a committee will receive the support of the government. That being so I have carefully considered the proper course for me to adopt, and have concluded that I should reserve my address on this matter until after the hearings of the committee and until after the committee has reported back to the house. I may say I have reached that conclusion most reluctantly, because I have been here day after day since the debate began, ready to speak on the motion before the house. But I submit that to be consistent with the best traditions of British parliamentary practice, the course I have decided to adopt is in all the circumstances the proper one. Let me make it clear however that at the proper time, when this matter returns to the floor of the house,
I propose to make a very definite and full statement with regard to the entire situation.
I do ask the committee composed of members of the house of all shades of political thought to meet and to deal with the matter with every possible dispatch.
Until parliament has finally passed upon the matter I submit harm is being done to workmen in Toronto and to Canada's relationship to the British empire in respect to that most vital problem of to-day, rearmament and defence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to participate in this debate or to speak respecting the Bren gun. But after listening to speeches made by hon. members of the opposition I felt I owed it to the people who have sent me to parliament as their representative, and to myself as well, to make some comments.
I suggest that the terms of reference to the public accounts committee should not be limited to circumstances surrounding the gun contract alone. The committee should have the widest possible powers to inquire into the entire, system of awarding government contracts. I am in complete accord with what was said on Monday last by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), that all these
contracts should be referred to the public accounts committee. The Star-Phoenix, a widely read newspaper in Saskatchewan, states in a leading editorial that we should go the whole way, that the reference should go deeper than simply making an inquiry into the Bren gun contract, and should cover the entire period from the great war to the present time.
I realize that on the order paper, in the name of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), there a resolution m which it is proposed to set up a defence purchasing board. I believe that board should have been set up at the very beginning. I was pleased yesterday to hear the minister say that that had been his idea, but that he had not so stated before the royal commissioner because as a responsible minister of the crown and a privy councillor he could not commit the government until he had consulted with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
I say there should be a most careful examination not only of this contract, but, as the Star-Phoenix has pointed out, of other contracts as well. Yet, the mere fact that this contract has been brought to public attention is no reason for the government to jump, like a fly on a hot griddle, to any extreme measures. If one method of procedure has been found to be irregular-and there is nothing so far which shows that it was- there is no assurance that any opposite method would be completely satisfactory. That is to say, if the government intends to embark upon a policy of manufacture by the government of implements of war, or if it is proposed to establish a public arsenal at Valcartier, the question arises whether or not the location would be proper from a strategic standpoint.
Might it not be well to have public arsenals situated throughout the length and breadth of Canada? If such arsenals were set up, to all intents and purposes the employees working in them would be civil servants. We would have to provide them with schools, churches, places of recreation and medical and dental attention. Of course, if the arsenals were erected in well established communities we would not have to supply those facilities, because they would already be provided. If the manufacture of war materials becomes a public venture, we should not have all our eggs in one basket, but should scatter them throughout the length and breadth of the dominion.
If I had been placed in a position similar to that of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) and an opportunity had been given to me to get work for the people in my
Bren Gun-Mr. Fleming

constituency, I am proud to say I would have been the first one to try to obtain that work for them, and would have raised heaven and earth in my efforts.
Many people seem to be of the opinion that any point in Canada would be a suitable place to set up one of these arsenals. May I point out, however, that in view of the advances which have been made in modem warfare, and particularly in air forces, we must be very careful to see that our arsenals are protected, and that they are placed at points where they will involve the least possible danger to the civilian population.
Then, too, the financial burden to be borne by the taxpayer must be considered. I have given the matter careful thought, and I can think of no place better suited for a public arsenal than the constituency of Humboldt, which I have the honour to represent. On various occasions in the house the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has said that the present government is trying to destroy private enterprise. Mr. Speaker, here is a private enterprise, and this government is not trying to destroy it. While I can well understand the stand taken by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, with their belief in complete public ownership, I do say, in answer to those who have tried to create in the minds of the electorate ideas for the advancement of their own political ends, that the Liberal party should not be intimidated into formulating a hasty policy.
If I thought there was anything wrong with the contract; if I thought there had been any graft or corruption in connection with it, I would rise in my place to oppose it. I am not hidebound to any political party. Since I have come to the House of Commons I have had a free rein. Never once since I have been a member has my leader, or the minister from Saskatchewan, or any other member of the government, suggested to me what particular line I should take in connection with any question which has come before the house. If I had anything against any member of the government I would not be afraid to take a pot shot at him.

With a Bren gun. After all, this royal commission that was set up made a searching and far-reaching investigation. The report has been quoted quite often, but I should like to quote shortly from page 52, as follows:
All the sittings of the commission were public and your commissioner was pleased to hear counsel characterize the inquiry, at its close, as "a most searching and thorough inquiry." 
After reading that statement and after listening to the dignified and gentlemanly statement made some days ago by the right hon. Prime Minister, I fail to see where any blame can be attached to any member of this house, any member of the government, to any member of the Liberal party no matter what lowly position he may occupy. From the moment Colonel George Drew's magazine article appeared, suspicion was created in the mind of the public that graft and corruption were rampant in connection with the awarding of government contracts. Frankly I think irreparable damage has been done by that article. I am sure that if this contract were suddenly to sprout wings, some people would not admit it past the portals of heaven.
Politics and politicians are always suspect because certain individuals in order to gain political preferment are always ready to sacrifice truth upon the altar of wild statements. Even the opposition is exposed to that. A few days ago the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) complained bitterly in this house that he had been accused of sabotage in connection with the Canadian National Railways. I would be willing to wager with him that for every person he finds who remembers his denial, he will find another who believes that there must be some truth in that allegation, otherwise it would never have been made. I am particularly concerned with this Bren gun contract because Maclean's magazine has a widespread circulation within my constituency. In his magazine article of September last, Colonel Drew made no direct charges. As the minister said, his article was filled with misstatements, half-truths and vicious innuendoes. No series of denials will ever wipe out entirely the bad taste which that article has left in the mouths of the Canadian electorate. It is just as difficult as trying to answer the question, "Have you stopped beating your wife?"
Without anticipating the findings of the public accounts committee, I wish to state emphatically that I believe the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence and all the officials of the government acted not only in good faith but in a manner which showed that they were attempting to obtain a good bargain and a good deal for the Canadian people. It must be remembered that we were in the initial stage of a development in connection with which Canada had little experience. The contract met with the approval of the British war office which has had hundreds of years of experience in, letting similar contracts.
Was there any reason to believe that the Canadian committee erred? That committee

Bren Gun-Mr. Fleming
was composed of a number of well known government officials. One member was a distinguished soldier and administrator, Major General LaFleche. Another member was Doctor O. D. Skelton, a former professor at Queen's university, from whom I learned my political philosophy. He is a man of the highest attainments and has been recognized as such by the leaders of both great political parties. Mr. Fraser Elliott, K.C., is a man who has few peers in his own field in the world. Doctor Clark is another former professor of political science at Queen's university whose capabilities are unquestioned. Surely no one can point the finger of scorn at any of these impartial civil servants.
It is difficult to understand why this storm over this contract has arisen except for the fact that it is meant to provide political capital. It is a bold-faced attempt to embarrass the government and the Minister of National Defence.

The same old game is being tried at the present time. They are trying to catch the government between the scissors of nationalism and the necessity of rearmament. The government has tried to create in the minds of the public the necessity for rearmament and to have all parts of Canada united. The3r are not trying to ostracize one part of this country.

If you will go back with me, sir, to 1923, you will find in
Bren Gun-Mr. Fleming

Maclean's magazine of July 1 of that year a most vile and vicious attack upon French Canada, one of the most vicious attacks that anj'one could ever read, and it appeared in a serial entitled, " The Bond Triumphant." That, Mr. Speaker, was in 1923, and if you will read that article and a few subsequent editions you will find that it had to be taken out of the magazine because it caused such a revulsion of public feeling across the.whole north American continent.
Is it any wonder, then, that that scandal sheet would print this scandalous article which Colonel Drew wrote to make a vicious attack upon the only French-Canadian deputy minister in the public service.

Mr.Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), in addressing the house last Thursday on his resolution, made it very clear to hon. members that the commissioner had placed squarely before parliament the following issues:
1.	Whether the Bren gun should be produced by the government in publicly-owned factories or through private manufacture.
2.	Whether the conduct of the individuals concerned was above question.
3.	Whether adequate reasons existed for the failure of the interdepartmental committee to report back to the government when the system of supervision of contracts broke down.
4.	Whether the procedure followed in negotiating this contract protected the public interest.
5.	Whether proper steps were taken to ensure discharge of the responsibility assumed in the selection of a favoured contractor.
A number of government supporters have repeatedly pointed out that no finding of misconduct has been made against any individual. But the commissioner makes it very clear, on page 34 of his report, that having in mind the limitations imposed on him by the statutory authority under which the inquiry was held-to use his own words-
I have come to the conclusion that it is inexpedient to comment upon the evidence in respect of its bearing on the conduct of the individuals concerned.
Therefore I say that in my opinion the government supporters are quite in error in suggesting that the absence of charges by the commissioner means lack of justification for charges.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking on February 6, said, as reported at page 679 of Hansard-.
I have yet to hear any condemnation of the contract itself from the individuals who have been addressing this house.
I have read the contract, and there are many features of it which I unhesitatingly condemn. But as my colleagues and others have thoroughly discussed most of the sections to which I also take exception, I shall deal only with the part relating to the stock transactions which finally resulted in the incorporation of the present John Inglis Company. This will involve the fourth point mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver North.
In order to make clear just what the commissioner thought about the stock transactions,
I am going to place on the record, if I may, an excerpt from the original evidence, at pages 956 to 961 of the record.
This question was asked by Mr. Forsyth, government counsel, of Mr. C. F. Elliott, dominion income tax commissioner.
Q. There was some mention in your cross examination-I am not going to quote it- which I should like to call to your memory.
Tt wee suggested to you that there were a number of shares outstanding, as per the Dun and Bradstreet report. You made an answer to my learned friend Mr. Drew in which you referred to the fact that a stopper had been put in. I just want you to explain what you mean by the word "stopper."
The Commissioner:	I think I observed to
the witness that his evidence disclosed that he had information-it may have been accurate- that the company had 220,000 shares issued.
I asked him if he had interested himself, or if the members of the committee had interested themselves in knowing who were the holders of those 220,000 shares. That observation was made after the witness had spoken of the relation between the number of shares and the $1,280,000. I have his answer on that, which I need not repeat. I do not know that anyone asked him, and I am quite willing for you to do so, if any effort was made in the public interest to avoid having those 220,000 shares becoming the subject matter of transactions, we will say, on the stock exchange.
Mr. Geoffrion:	There is no evidence that
they will become the subject of transactions.
The Commissioner:	I am just asking if he
anticipated any such thing, or if the committee anticipated providing any protection. I see there is a clause in the contract and if you want to read that it will be all right. However, I do not think it has any bearing on my question at all.
Mr. Forsyth: I do not think you are referring to the same examination, Mr. Commissioner. I remember that Mr. Elliott developed the idea that the company could increase its capital and so on.
The Commissioner:	They have protected
against that by providing a clause in the contract that the company is not to issue or sell any shares, bonds, securities, etc., of the company, directly or indirectly, without the approval of the government. But that does not in any way affect the 220,000 shares issued and outstanding. The question I was trying to ask the witness this morning-I left the answer then because of the thought that they had no interest really in the directors or shareholders. What I was getting at was the fact that these 220,000 shares might be sold publicly on the market at a future date and I wanted to know if the committee visualized that problem and if they took any competent measures in the public interest to control that situation so that there would be no public trading of those shares.
Mr. Forsyth then questioned the witness as follows:
Q. Mr. Elliott, you used the word "stopper" in connection with this, and I presume you were referring to a clause in the contract. Have yor the contract before you?
A. Yes.
m

Bren Gun-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
Q. Would you indicate the number of the clause to which you were referring? Am I correct in assuming that you were referring to a clause as a stopper? .
A. Oh, yes. That is correct. It is the second paragraph of section 1. Shall I read it?
Q. If you do not mind.
A. This is a proviso which reads:
"Provided further, that notwithstanding the provisions of anything herein contained, the said licence shall be subject to cancellation if in the course of the period thereof the party of the second part should sell shares, stocks, bonds, debentures, notes or other like securities to the public, directly or indirectly, or through the medium of other companies the proceeds of which are not directly applied to the business of the party of the second part and there remain applicable for use in the carrying on of said party's business, then the licence shall cease unless before the issue of such security instruments the consent to the issue thereof has first been secured from the party of the first part."
Mr. Drew:	That section obviously has no
relation whatever to the 220,000 shares you have mentioned?
The Commissioner: Of course it is subject to argument, but it is perfectly plain that that clause refers to the issue by the company and sale by the company. I am not stopping you, Mr. Forsyth, but I must tell you that I am still groping in the dark to find out whether the committee ever visualized the problem that there was a possibility or a probability that the then issue of 220,000 shares out of the total authorized of 250.000 shares might become the subject matter of trading on the public exchanges or in a private way as war stock. I want to know if the committee ever visualized that and, if so, what did they do?
Mr. Forsyth: You have heard the discussion-
He is still questioning Mr. Elliott.
-and the question raised as to the possible disposition of the 220.000 shares of stock issued, as per the Dun and Bradstreet report. The possibility was mentioned in your cross-examination this morning of a further increased capital. The point now is: Did the committee visualize-to use the commissioner's words- dealings in the 220.000 shares already issued and which might be objectionable, from the public point of view? Is that a fair way to put it, Mr. Commissioner?
The Commissioner: Yes.
The Witness: They visualized that and many other related matters of a similar character.
By the Commissioner:
Q. In what way did you deal with it?
A. By inserting in the paragraph which I have just read.
Q. That is your answer to the question?
A. I would-
Q. That is either the protection you took or it is not?
A. That is the protection we took after discussing it at great length.
Q. As a merpber of the committee you had it in your mind that that was sufficient protection for the problem which you say you envisaged?
A. When you say "sufficient protection," if I were writing that myself I would catch the ideas as we had them presented that night in the committee. I would write it out and I would polish it and re-polish it until it would

contain fully all our views and all my comprehensions as to the various ways in which capital could be sold to the public, either by writing up the present stock, increasing it and so on. So that when you ask me if that was completely my idea or the committee's, the answer technically is, No. We would have liked to have had time to polish and re-polish it, but we had to pass it that night. I hope it carries the main idea of a means of stopping it, but technically I could not say that it is perfection. '
Q. Whatever your thoughts were that night, they must be plain to you now that that clause does not affect or attempt to affect the sale of the then issued 220,000 shares?
A. Not the 220,000, no, but it would affect, I think, a split of them and issuing three for one or something like that. That is perhaps a question of interpretation.
Mr. Forsyth: As a matter of fact I do not know that I would agree with you, Mr. Commissioner, or with the witness on that. I think it is a subject for later argument.
The Commissioner: I think it is as plain as day. I do not think there is any use splitting hairs as to what it says.
That is the opinion of the commissioner as to the protection of the public in the matter of disposing of the vendors' shares. I was surprised at the absence in the commissioner's report, of any extended comment on the stock transactions, but apparently he had in mind two things. The first was the limitations I have already referred to which he believed were imposed upon him by the statute under which the inquiry was held, and the second would probably be the fact that he did not want to clash with the jurisdiction of the Ontario securities commission. The great insistence of various counsel upon the point of there not being any comment indicated to me beyond question that they were perfectly well aware what kind of comment the commissioner would make if he felt privileged to do so. Anyone who reads the evidence and arguments of counsel relating to the financial and stock transactions, and noting the commissioner's comments thereon, will not be left in doubt as to what he thought. A clear profit of over 81,000,000 in the stock transactions alone plus 8467,000 of operating profit under the two contracts, or total profits of at least 81,467,000 on an investment which, including the proceeds of sale of treasury stock, was not more than $500,000, means profits of 285 per cent on that transaction. How could that be described as other than one of the most heartless and barefaced pieces of profiteering in the history of Canada? And this is the contract which the minister has described as one of the finest. If it is correct, that this is one of the finest contracts ever signed by the department, I tremble to think what we shall find when we come to look into others.

Bren Gun-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
To show that the government was in possession of complete information and knowledge as to how to prevent stock watering and excessive profits, I wish to place on the record part of a memorandum furnished the interdepartmental committee by Mr. Elliott, dominion income tax commissioner. Mr. Elliott explained that during the great war the department had considered the various ways by which firms and individuals who were profiteering out of war contract? had sought to evade payment of income tax. Among other things he therefore proposed the following in reference to the amount of capital to be employed. He said:
Let the amount of capital to be invested by the contractor be predetermined, certified by recognized authorities and approved by government officials before or at the time the contracts are made. Thus, inflation of capital assets, goodwill and other undesirable tendencies after the contract has been given might be avoided, and also there might be avoided an unfair and excessive profit based on inflated values. Make certain that the value behind the share is cash, or an asset having real value.
At page 2294 of the evidence, government counsel questioned the minister about this report. Mr. Ralston, examining the minister, asked:
Q. Now, Mr. Mackenzie, that report was transmitted to you. What did you do with it?
A. I carefully perused it personally-it was of great interest to me.
But after coming into possession of this carefully prepared information, which showed in precise detail exactly how to prevent this stock watering, what did the minister do? Well, the evidence shows that he did everything possible to assist this contractor in accomplishing his purpose. Despite the fact that the minister had repeatedly declared his belief in the public ownership and operation of plants for the manufacture of war materials-at page 10 of the commissioner's report we read that the minister said, in reply to a question by Mr. Hellmuth, that he believed in public ownership through and through-the evidence shows that his department exercised constant and unremitting pressure on the war office in England to have them negotiate a contract with Major Hahn, a private manufacturer, who had neither the equipment nor the experience to do the work. Evidence of this will be found on page 48 of the commissioner's report. Speaking in the House of Commons on April 2, 1937, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said:
We agree with him in asserting the principle that no profits should be made out of war.
At page 2148 of the evidence, I quote as follows from a memorandum sent by the chief
of general staff to the master general of ordnance, under date July 11, 1936:
I still feel that a small arms and munition factory should be established capable of making revolvers, rifles, and automatic rifles including the Bren gun.
Why, in the face of all this, did the government not carry out its own publicly professed policy and the advice of its own technically competent civil service advisers? Surely no informed person would dare to denv that public opinion, in Canada is overwhelmingly in favour of eliminating profits from the manufacture of war materials. The only reason given by the minister is, to use his own words as quoted in the report at page 11, "financial stringency." Yet he signs a contract with a private manufacturer under which the Canadian taxpayers furnish this man with a complete outfit of machinery; pay him $10,000 a year, and in addition provide him and his associates with stock watering profits of over $1,000,000 and an enormous operating profit as well.
I have listened with amazement during this week, as speaker after speaker has unfolded this story of the plunder of the Canadian people, with the active assistance of the government. I want publicly to thank Colonel Drew for bringing this matter to light. At both the 1937 and 1938 sessions I placed resolutions on the order paper demanding that a committee be set up to study this very question, but each year parliament prorogued without even discussing it. Now we find that these shameful things were going on at that very time. Speaking in the house on Tuesday, February 16, 1937, just two years ago, I referred to the profits made during the last war by private firms in both the United States and Canada. I pointed out how twenty-two meat packing firms, sixteen cotton yam manufacturers, thirty-nine garment manufacturers, fifteen steel plants and rolling mills, and 135 coal producers in the United States reported to the government profits of 100 per cent or more, while twenty-one firms reported profits of over 500 per cent but under 1,000 per cent, and fourteen firms reported profits of over
1,000	per cent. I pointed out also how 21,000 new millionaires were created in the United States and between 600 and 700 new millionaires in Canada. And while this was going on, every day while the great war lasted, 20,000 men and boys were killed, wounded or taken prisoner, and during the course of the conflict 40,000,000 people died of wounds, famine and pestilence. To meet the total cost of the war, $337,000,000,000, would require a payment of $20,000 an hour from the birth of Christ to the end of the world war. Then, with particular reference to profiteering in Canada I said:

Bren Gun-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
What guarantee can the government give that there will be no war profiteering? What assurance is there that at this very moment our natural resources are not being turned into instruments of war? What firms in Canada are at present engaged in the manufacture of armaments, munitions and war supplies for Great Britain or any other countries? What profits are actually being reaped by Canadian concerns through the provision of such materials? And-perhaps more serious than all else-what guarantee have we that our youth will not be expected to face the very arms and be targets for the very munitions that are now being exported from this country?
The government did not answer these questions; they were not willing to take even a few days to investigate them in accordance with the terms of my resolution. I am therefore supporting the motion to refer this contract to the public accounts committee, where I hope we shall be given an opportunity to investigate these matters fully.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), speaking in Edmonton on March 6, 1938, is reported in the Edmonton Bulletin of March 7 as having stated, "The real evil is an unequal and uneven distribution of purchasing power," and he added, " Progressive Liberalism, animated by its basic belief in ' equality of opportunity and equality of sacrifice ' will relentlessly labour for a more equitable distribution of wealth." And the paper added that this statement was made amid ringing applause. I wonder whether that audience would have applauded so loudly if they had realized that, as a result of the policies of the Liberal party, after seventy years of " relentless labour" in support of those policies, at the very moment the hon. gentleman was speaking, 4,000 families in Canada were receiving average incomes of $150,000 a year each, 16,000 families were receiving an average of $39,000 a year each, 536 persons had in their bank accounts, on an average, $287,500 each, while at the other end of the scale Canada's 3,000,000 farmers were receiving an average income per family of $474, and 98 per cent of all the wage-earners in Canada were receiving an average income of $668 a year. The way the minister " labours relentlessly " for a more equitable distribution of Canadian wealth, based upon " equality of opportunity and equality of sacrifice," is to hand a fat contract to a bunch of stockbrokers, lawyers and armament racketeers to enable them to plunder the Canadian people out of a million dollar stock watering profit, besides enormous operating profits, to be added to their already large incomes.
Why is it that public opinion on this continent is so thoroughly aroused against profiteering in armament making? In my opinion it is undoubtedly on account of the

wide publicity given to the Nye committee findings in the United States, and to disclosures made in the French Chamber of Deputies and the British House of Commons. And Colonel Drew, in his article in Maclean's magazine and others which he has written in the past, and other writers of books and articles, have done a great deal to arouse public opinion -by bringing these matters to light. It was because of this aroused public opinion that our representatives at the League of Nations assembly have always advocated public ownership and operation of armament factories. We all know the story of Sir Basil Zaharoff, who made a fortune estimated at from two hundred million to a billion dollars from the sale of the instruments of death, and as a reward was knighted by the British government; how he was consulted in 1917 when there was a possibility of achieving peace through the intervention of the United States, and Lord Bertie, British ambassador to France, recorded in his diary, " Zaharoff is all for continuing the war jusqu'au bout." It is not surprising that an armament racketeer should want to continue a murder racket out of which he was making millions of dollars a month, but how do we explain the fact that he was a close confidant of the British Prime Minister; that he was consulted as to whether or not the war should go on; that he was knighted by the same Prime Minister as a reward for his " services " and that later from the hundreds of millions of dollars reaped in that harvest of death out of the blood, tears, agony, disease, debt and death of the world's common people, he endowed chairs in literature at Oxford university and the Sor-bonne, naming them the "Foch" and "Haig" chairs to perpetuate his gory fame?
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know of any occasion in the House of Commons which is just as important as the one that is before the house in this debate. I say that because it is probably one occasion, and possibly the only one, when a major party in the house

Bren Gun-Mr. McGeer
has refused to accept the findings of a royal commission as determining an important public matter in an extremely critical time not only for our own nation but for the peace of the whole world.
When the matter first arose it came in the form of an article published by an outstanding Canadian public man in a journal of general circulation throughout the dominion. It was probably one of the most critical articles that had ever been published in condemnation of a minister of the crown and a department responsible for the defence of the nation. The course taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has been commended by everyone.
This article, not by formulated charge but by innuendo and inference, was, I think, intended to and, I firmly believe, did convey to the minds of everyone who read it that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) was unworthy of public confidence; that there had been a granting of contractual privileges and an expediture of public moneys that were not merely negligent but fraudulent and designed to injure the public well-being and the public treasury for the benefit of persons preferred as friends of the administration.
It is true that since this debate has developed in the house, and after the findings of the commission, the more moderate attitude adopted by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has been taken. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) also changed from the attitude of the article. I want to say that innuendo can be more deadly against public men than direct charges, because there is no limitation to the imagination aroused by innuendo, and there is nothing defined for the one suspected to meet. So we find the leader of the opposition declaring, "I am not charging corruption, neither is George Drew doing so."
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is not in line with the statements of the distinguished colonel. He is on record. Let us look at what he has to say about General LaFleche, the deputy minister of national defence and one of Canada's most distinguished veterans. He has been described by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George as "the most honourable of men." Let us look at the record. At page 4300, in his charge to the commission, Colonel Drew says:
Whether it be from the point of view of business interests, industrial efficiency or national security, nothing can be said, I submit, to justify this contract in any way. It was conceived in sin, born in iniquity and cloaked in fraud.

The commissioner finds that it was abundantly clear that long before the Bren gun contract was ever thought of, Major Hahn and his associates were negotiating for the purchase of the John Inglis plant. The John Inglis company plant consists of fourteen different buildings. It was the outstanding Canadian munitions plant during the last war, and its engineers declare that to-day its equipment is in better shape than it ever was.
What did Major Hahn do? Did he go to England and depend upon the letter of introduction and recommendation from Canada? No, not at all. He took with him a complete book of photographs showing every detail of the plant he proposed to use. He took with him, according to the findings of the commissioner, the blue-prints of every building and of every machine, and the capacity of each of them. He took also the reference of his bankers, the Bank of Montreal, of Canada. These records of the plant were handed over to the officials of the war department at Enfield for investigation. It was in the light of that situation, the placing of the facts openly before the war office, that he was able to secure the confidence of the war office officials, and on November 9, almost a year after they had secured the ownership of the plant in Toronto, to have a telegram forwarded to the Department of National Defence that the war office were prepared to let a contract to the John Inglis Company for 5,000 guns.

I do hope this matter will go to the public accounts committee so that it may be dealt with on its merits. I do hope that the house will recognize the seriousness of the situation which exists, and that it will also recognize that there are great problems of social needs, great problems of human welfare, great problems of municipal needs and other problems of development with which we might deal, and that this matter	will	not	be allowed	tomonopolize more	time	than	is necessary	tobring our national defence system into the highest state of	perfection.	The people	ofCanada are expecting the House of Commons to move into action on all the problems of the day, and we shall do little but serve the subversive forces of the nation if we haggle in parliament over partisan advantage. There are hustings for	that	kind	of thing. The
hustings would have been the place for most of the speeches we have heard from the opposition in this debate.
A little later on I hope to pay my tribute to the Minister of National Defence, to the deputy minister, to the Department of National Defence and to this government for the great change that has been made during the last few years in the defensive forces of this country. I believe that out of this debate will come a need for greater defensive power, a need which for the time being at least will compel us to forget the balancing of budgets and come to a realization that as other nations have found a need of great programs of 71492-52
defence and great programs of service, we in Canada must go along with the times and see that our monetary technique as well as our defence technique are adjusted to the needs of the nation.

I can well remember
when there was not so much cheering after a speech by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). They put up the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot), and the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). What did they say in their speeches? Prime Minister, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. I want to tell the hon. member for Temiscouata that the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett is going to bring great honour to this country.
