speechtext:
Let me tell the hon.
member who has just spoken that not only did the mayor have the support of the hon. members I have mentioned, but he was elected by the Liberal vote in Montreal and by the promise of this government to spend $12,000,000 on that hole in that city. That was the statement he made on the night of his election. The hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard told us to-night that others had a chance to get this contract. No one knew about the contract except Major Hahn. The members of the Liberal party who have spoken claim there was no reason for competition, but in spite of the advice which came to the Minister of National Defence from various sources which I shall enumerate, the contract was given to a private corporation.
First of all, we had a fine interdepartmental committee set up for this very purpose, and they recommended that the contract be awarded by tender. Second, we have Major

General Ashton, chief of the general staff, recommending a government-owned factory. Third, we have the British government insisting that the Bren gun be manufactured in a government-owned plant. Fourth, and not least, we have the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) recommending that tenders be called, and we have the Minister of National Defence agreeing with him. Let me quote from page 11 of the report to bear out my statement. Speaking in the House of Commons on April 2, 1937, the Prime Minister had this to say regarding munitions contracts:
At the present time, in a time of peace, the government is proceeding on the theory of permitting competition with reasonable remuneration, the work to be subject to inspection and audit. . . . We agree with him in asserting the principle that no profits should be made out of war.
I am sure every hon. member agrees with that. Then we have the Minister of National Defence agreeing with the Prime Minister. In his evidence before the commission the minister stated that that statement of the Prime Minister was in agreement with his own views. Yet when it came to awarding the contract they did not adopt that course. Why? Well might	we	ask	why,	and	thecountry at large is asking why. It appears that the reason was that the Minister of National Defence seemed set on giving the contract to Major Hahn. The minister in his evidence said that no one had asked for a contract. I think that is a most childish answer. Let me read the minister's evidence. He was answering	questions put	by	Mr. Hellmuth. Mr. Hellmuth asked:
You did not give anybody else a chance?
And the minister's answer was:
Nobody asked for	it.
Nobody asked for	it!	Mr.	Hellmuth went
on:
Q. Mr. Minister, what I want to get you to answer is this: You never did attempt in any method or any way to see what any one of these dozen or more well known companies, with skilled labour, skilled mechanics, who had been working in precision steel-well, let us take the automobile industry which makes the very closest parts and closest tolerances-no effort was made of any kind to see what they could do?
And the minister's answer to that was:
No.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that this is a peculiar way for any government to do business. There is a contract to be let; a member of parliament brings down a man, introduces him, and he gets the contract.

Bren Gun-Mr. Hyndman
Let us look at the contract and let us look at Major Hahn. I quote from page 15 of the report:
On seeing the gun both of them (Mr. Plaxton and Major Hahn) went over to it, looked at it and asked what it was. I told them it was the new Bren gun. I do not believe that either of them had ever seen the gun.
Some man to give the contract to for manufacturing the Bren gun when he had never seen it before! It was a man by the name of Major Hahn who was brought down and introduced by a member of parliament to the deputy minister, a man who, as has often been pointed out here, was a radio salesman. He had bought, I will not say an old boiler factory, but a boiler factory which had been closed, and he formed a company, which I must say at the present time looks a fairly good investment. The company consists mostly of Major Hahn with a few office boys and girls, and they will make on the 191,622 shares of stock alone, if they sell them at $7.50 a share, $1,341,634. I consider that really good business.
But what strikes me most in this report is that the Minister of National Defence did not know Major Hahn, and he did not know what was going on. I prove that by quoting from page 28 of the report, where Mr. Hell-muth is questioning the Minister of National Defence:
Q. I am asking you if you knew the personnel of the reliable group?
A. No.
Q. You did not know that?
A. No.
Q. I would like to have that question answered, with all due deference. I would like to know whether you knew whether Major Hahn had or controlled any plant or plants?
A. Not to my own knowledge-certainly not.
Q. Do you know whether he had any company at that time?
A. Not to my knowledge, no.
Q. When dill you find out that Major Hahn had associates, and who they were?
A. I did not know who they were until the article referred to in this investigation (i.e., Maclean's magazine).
So thank goodness that Colonel Drew, who has been under criticism in this house, did write that article because at least he drew this man Hahn to the attention of the Minister of National Defence. The evidence continues:
Q. So that we may say the contract-at the time the contract was signed you had no knowledge of who his associates were?
A. That is quite correct.
I think that proves, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Defence-and he takes responsibility for this contract; he cannot
blame it on his deputy or anybody else- knew absolutely nothing about the contract and knew nothing about Major Hahn.
Let us look at the contract. As far as I can see, from looking over the contract, it has been drawn up by capable lawyers, and I venture to say that technically it is sound. But if I were a manufacturer I would be pleased indeed to get a contract such as this, because according to it, as I figure it out, the government provides everything and Hahn gets the cream. And who is he getting the cream from? He is getting it from the taxpayers of this country. They are the ones who are going to pay the bill. And what confidence, I ask, are the Canadian people going to have in the minister and in the Department of National Defence when he comes to parliament and asks for $63,000,000 to be spent on national defence?
I am going to make two recommendations. They are recommendations that have already been made. They are very brief, and I agree with both of them.
First, I am going to make the recommendation that Mr. Justice Davis makes on page 51 of his report, where he says:
The purchase or production of such munitions or armaments should be put into the hands of an expert advisory group of competent business men-a capable and experienced manufacturer, a commercial lawyer who has had a wide practice in dealing with large commercial contracts, a representative of labour, and say a chartered accountant who has had experience in the examination of substantial business transactions. These persons should constitute a board (which might be known as the "defence purchasing board") and be made directly accountable to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Finance.
In that last sentence the commissioner is advising the setting up of a board responsible to whom? Responsible to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. If he could see nothing the matter with this contract, why did he not say that the board should be responsible to the Minister of National Defence? But no, he advises that it be taken out of the hands of the Minister of National Defence and put under the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.
The other suggestion is this:	We have the
Prime Minister in the speech from the throne suggesting that at this session-[DOT]
Legislation will be introduced .to establish a defence purchasing board with power to purchase equipment for the defence services and to ensure that, where private manufacture is necessary, profits in connection with such are fair and reasonable, and that the public interest is protected.
Bren Gun-Mr. Hyndman

I contend that these two statements, the one from the Prime Minister and the other from Mr. Justice Davis, are enough in themselves to cause criticism of the workings of the Department of National Defence. I agree with the suggestion that has been made by my honoured leader. I would not go so far as to say that the Minister of National Defence or his deputy should be discharged, because in a way they-especially the minister-knew nothing of what was going on, but I will say, and I. think the Prime Minister will find that the people are demanding it, that this contract must be cancelled. We must restore the confidence of the people in the national defence department. One has only to refer to what happened in the old country. When inefficiency was shown in the department [DOT]charged with defence matters, the British Prime Minister was not long in discharging the responsible minister, Sir Thomas Inskip. To restore the confidence of the people in the department, I repeat, this contract must be cancelled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by reason of certain statements made during the course of the debate I am prompted to say a word or two in an attempt to clarify certain issues. I moved the motion of reference to the public accounts committee, and in doing so, endeavoured to state in the simplest possible terms the reasons for the introduction of that motion. The debate since that time has traversed a very wide field, a much wider field than was anticipated. I desire, as I have said, as briefly and simply as possible to bring the discussion back to the central issues, issues which have been largely disregarded, issues which have not been fully and adequately explained and concerning which in some respects no explanation at all has been offered by supporters of the government's policy.
I feel it necessary to explain to the house the motives which prompted me to discuss this contract. I do so because the suggestion has been made by hon. gentlemen opposite that this has been something of a monstrous conspiracy to embarrass the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), to defame his character, and to harass him at this time as he is attempting to repair the defences of this dominion.
There is no such conspiracy. But if the minister is in touch with public opinion to-day; if he is alert to discern what is taking place throughout the country, he must realize that this very effort he has made to make Canada defence-conscious has, by the same token,

impressed upon the country the importance of his duties and responsibilities. A strict accounting may be demanded for every move he makes, because of the extraordinary power he wields at this time on behalf of the dominion.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) took pains to refer to the Ross rifle deal in the last war. It is significant that he did so, in view of the fact that the veiy machinery which manufactured the Ross rifle has been shipped to the factory of the John Inglis Company in Toronto.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOK REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should just like to point out, in view of some newspaper publicity which has been given to the idea just now expressed, that what I stated was that you require more than machinery in order to make good guns of any kind, and Mr. Hahn was an addition to the machinery.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOK REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well, the minister can
explain his own statement. I just said it was significant he referred to that in view of the fact that the machinery used in manufacturing the Ross rifle was shipped to the John Inglis Company in Toronto. I mention this to point out that this deal is almost on all fours with the Ross rifle deal of years ago: that at that time there was the definite determination to rely on private manufacture; that at that time there was the definite effort to secure a complementary order from the British government; that the deal was proceeded with by the Canadian government of that day largely because of patronage considerations, with the result that British government inspectors were rejecting rifles which were issued to the Canadian troops-issued with results which were well known to all those who served in the great war.
If the house will pardon a personal reference, I desire to say that I was privileged to serve as a machine gunner in the last war. The machine guns with which we were originally equipped were provided by private manufacture; and in looking up the record of this house, the journals, and copies of the orders in council dealing with the purchase of the machine guns, I find that through patronage influence sales were made in opposition to the opinion of the British war office. What was the result? I participated in the result, and for that reason I am concerned as to the outcome of the deal which we are discussing to-day. At a crucial moment, when we were required to protect the infantry occupying a position which was almost untenable, we could not make four guns do the work of one under

Bren Gun-Mr. MacNeil
active service conditions, by reason of faults in design, construction and manufacture; and the mudholes which we occupied at that time became a veritable shambles because of the failure of that equipment to operate. Prominent senior officers were cashiered over that episode, and I should not be blamed by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence if I hold vividly in recollection the memory of comrades who went gallantly to their deaths because they were furnished with faulty equipment by private manufacture resulting from a deal of this kind.
I have in mind a conversation with a gentleman having some responsibility to the reading public of this country, who introduced himself to me. " MacNeil," he said, " I hope this matter will be cleared up to the satisfaction of the people of Canada. Despite all rumours in circulation as to my motives in giving some publicity to sensational statements, I want to make clear my personal interest in this matter. I have a son, MacNeil, of military age, and God forbid that he should be called upon to serve in the defence of this country while the back-door of the Department of National Defence is open to a lot of grafting leeches." And I said, "Amen." Many hon. members in all quarters of the house echo " amen " in their hearts in regard to such a situation. The point at issue is this, that a department susceptible to influences made manifest through the negotiations leading up to the execution of this contract, is certainly a department susceptible to influences which led to such ghastly results in 1915.
I am reminded of the statement made in this house by a gentleman who was then the member for Red Deer when he pleaded with the Prime Minister of the day to take suitable action that the gaze of the men in the field would not be turned on the horrors exposed in the public accounts committee of 1915.
I did hope that instead of the undignified performance in this house to-night by the Minister of National Defence, he would, by some guarantee, some frank explanation, by action rather than by blustering rhetoric; assure the people of Canada that there would be no recurrence of the terrible state of affairs which existed in 1915. When hon. gentlemen opposite say that charges should be made beyond those already contained in the commissioner's report, I wonder if our standard is lower than it was in 1915. It is within the memory of members of this house that when the seventh report of the public accounts committee was tabled in 1915 and the motion for concurrence was made a short
debate ensued in which Sir Robert Borden and Sir Wilfrid Laurier participated; and the then Prime Minister of Canada rose in his place and made it clear and unmistakable that he would not condone or compromise in any way with any suggestion of irregularity or fraud in war purchases. Although no charges were formulated; although no members had been named up to that time, as far as I am aware, he expressed his grave disapproval of the actions of two well-known members of his party, with the result that they were drummed out of public life.
If one reads the memoirs of Sir Robert Borden it is interesting to note that he made it clear that he would not only refuse to compromise with irregularity in the matter of war purchases but would insist, as in fact he did insist, and so instructed the Minister of Militia and the then Solicitor General, that there should be no dealings with middlemen, brokers and promoters, and that their profits would have to be cut out. And never have his political opponents suggested anything against his personal integrity. On many occasions, acting as Minister of Militia, he did enforce his rulings in that regard.
I trust that the Prime Minister will make available to succeeding generations important documents in regard to which a full disclosure may not be made at this time, in order that the verdict of history may deal fairly with the crises of our day. But I do appeal to him that a definite guarantee be given now, a guarantee which has not yet been given, and that a frank and full explanation be made. All that I ask is a clean deal for men who may have to take arms in defence of the country. But there is no clean, straightforward dealing when we have, as we now have, financial manipulation, bartering with company promoters and lack of faith in established Canadian industries.
I do not wish to prolong this discussion, but the Minister of National Defence suggested in the course of the debate that no one has done more than I have to destroy defence. Surely he did not mean that. I share his pride in highland Scotch ancestry and his pride in the contribution made by the highland Scotch to the upbuilding of this dominion. I am not so certain that I have the same pride after listening to the emotional outbursts which to-night characterized almost his entire speech. I also share with him appreciation of the fine qualities of our French-Canadian compatriots, but if he reads carefully the record of the statements that I have made in this house he will recognize that
Bren Gun-Mr. MacNeil

I have never, at any time, opposed all defence. I could not be disloyal because of the very roots of my existence. I am Canadian-born and the background of all my activities is associated with the development and welfare of this country. I have stated repeatedly that it is the responsibility of any government to provide reasonable defence against external danger, but I did question defence expenditures because of the lack of policy which made it impossible to distinguish between defence and offence. I also questioned the competency of officers because of the definite evidence similar to that which is now disclosed in the commissioner's report, that men in high places disregarded the policies enunciated in, and accepted in good faith by, the House of Commons.
The minister says that there is not even the shadow of political patronage in connection with this contract. May I ask him: If there was no political patronage, why did he take this matter in 1936 out of the hands of the interdepartmental committee set up by the Prime Minister to guarantee the Canadian public against such deals, and practically until 1938 refrain from consultation with that committee with respect to the particular contract which was negotiated? Why did he delay consultation with that committee until he was committed to a contract with the John Inglis *Company? What conclusion can we reach after reading the evidence given before the commissioner, when we read of the way in which Major Hahn was introduced to the department under the most favourable political auspices? Major Hahn wanted the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) to accompany him to England because he might be useful, and suggested that his expenses might be paid. These facts appear in the evidence which has been tabled. How can he possibly deny that there is any shadow of political patronage? What evidence has he introduced to refute the statements made on this side that political patronage was the predominating consideration throughout the negotiations prior to 1938? The minister carefully refrained from giving an explanation with regard to the main issue. My respect for the minister would have mounted considerably if he had taken the issues one by one and made a frank statement and explanation.
He said in this house, as on the stand, that he stood for the policy of public manufacture so far as the primary implements of war are concerned. This country was committed at Geneva to the public manufacture of armaments. The Prime Minister has repeatedly assured the house that he intended to pursue
{Mr. MacNeil.]
such a policy. That is the issue, an issue which the minister made no attempt tp discuss. He did not explain why he deviated from the policy of public manufacture. It is true he mentioned the limitation of appropriations made by parliament. He said he had an estimate furnished him that called for $30,000,000 or $35,000,000, and when that was traced to the minutes of the defence council it was found that the estimate related to a group of manufacturing establishments that would meet the entire requirements of all the Canadian forces. The evidence of the chief of general staff and of other senior officers shows that they urged, as the British government urged, for public manufacture in factories operated and controlled by the government. Without an explanation to the public he abandoned only too readily the policy which he enunciated in the house.
No explanation has been given by the minister as to why he deserted the system of competitive bids. He said on the stand that it was the next best alternative to public manufacture. Why, then, did he abandon it when the interdepartmental committee set up by the Prime Minister to protect the public interest urged repeatedly that comparative prices be obtained? He has challenged us from time to time to name firms competent to manufacture Bren guns. Well, the experts on the interdepartmental committee named five or six firms. After a survey made of industrial institutions, government plants, in this country, why did he not seek to avail himself of the machine shops under the control of the government-for example, the machine shop at Prescott equipped for the production of lighthouse instruments, the machine shops of the Canadian National Railways, the equipment already at Yalcartier and Lindsay?
And he proceeds to declare, without relation to the evidence, that this contract has saved this country something like a million and a half. It does not require a lawyer or an expert accountant, but just a little common sense, to understand the situation. Consider the evidence given by Gillespie, who has been quoted frequently. Gillespie explained that at Enfield they had two years investigation and testing in cooperation with the factory in Czechoslovakia and when they proceeded to manufacture the component parts of the Bren gun at Enfield they found themselves practically half-way there, because they had the machinery and equipment. I should like to hear the minister explain why, with any established firm as suggested by the interdepartmental committee, it would not be possible to use the equipment they had for

Bren Gun-Mr. MacNeil
working with precision steel, provide them with the equipment that the government had at Valcartier, with reimbursement as promised in the contract by joint arrangement with the British government for new machinery required, and secure deliveries at a much earlier date than possible with the John Inglis Company.
In this connection I am interested in the manner in which the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) skirted round this point in quoting from the evidence. Speaking of the ability of the John Inglis Company to manufacture this Bren gun, as reported on page 720 of Hansard, he quoted from the evidence given by Gillespie. No one questioned Gillespie's competency, but I point out that in reading his evidence it is clear that Gillespie was referring then only to the ability of three engineers, Ainsworth, MacLaghlan and Gazey. He said they were quick on the uptake; sure they were, 100 per cent; but that had nothing to do with the ability of the John Inglis Company to go on with the manufacture, because a few pages further on in the evidence he states that they were making satisfactory progress and perhaps they might be able to make deliveries according to schedule. Why are these matters not dealt with more frankly?

no adequate explanation with reference to the definite statement of the commissioner that the system of supervising the contracts broke down. The minister said in answer to a question in the house yesterday that he had received reports from the interdepartmental committee and he transmitted those reports to the defence committee of the cabinet. At page 2364 of the evidence he is reported as saying:
The only report I ever received was from the deputy minister who was chairman of the interdepartmental committee.
And we find him referring definitely to the fact that the minister received reports not from the committee as such but from the deputy minister in relation to the activities of the committee.
I see, Mr. Speaker, it is eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In regard to
to-morrow's business I assume the first order will be to continue the present debate. That will be the first motion called. But Friday is not a very good day on which to take a division of the house on as important a matter as this, and I understand a number of hon. members would much prefer that the debate should be continued on Monday rather than to-morrow. Therefore it would be the government's intention to-morrow, after the hon. member who has just spoken has finished his remarks, to have someone follow and adjourn this debate and then continue with the orders of the day which appear under government orders.
In that connection I should like to ask hon. members whether, provided we get through the government orders before the day is over, they would not permit us to go into committee of supply to take up some of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of National Revenue.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The only object of asking this is to expedite the business of the house. We can easily adjourn the house if that is preferable to hon. members, but I

would point out that so far the government has not been able to take up one single item of business. We have been here over four weeks and all the time has been taken up with private discussions; there has not been one item of government business taken up thus far. I am asking if we might begin tomorrow with supply if we get through the few resolutions which are on the order paper.

I do not wish to start
an argument at this time of night, but the right hon. gentleman says we have not taken up any public business. I consider this the most important business-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I did not say public business, I said government business. I am pointing out that we have now had a month in which private members have practically had control of the house, and the government have had no chance to get on with any of its business. We should like, if we can, to fill out a full day to-morrow, if that is agreeable. We are, however, entirely in the hands of the house.
It is understood then that to-morrow, after the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) has finished his remarks, this debate is adjourned until Monday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will be adjourned by the speaker who follows him. What about supply? Is there any objection on the part of hon. members to having supply taken up to-morrow-not more than one item? We need not take the whole day; but what the government would like to do is to run through the order paper, paying attention to those items appearing under government orders. We would not take up the act to amend the Pension Act, but we could take up the other two bills on the order paper. Then we could consider the resolutions which are there, exclusive of the one respecting the defence purchasing board. Then, when we have concluded the resolutions, if time permits we would like to occupy the balance of the day with the committee of supply, Department of Agriculture.
Is the Prime Minister not rather optimistic in thinking he can get through all those resolutions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I may be, but I do not think they are contentious.
Some of them are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If they are, of course we shall not get into supply.
